entries.title: After an injury, wait a week longer than you think and test one exercise at a time
entries.take: McDonald's two rules: when it feels healed, give it another week, then bring back one set of one exercise at a time.
entries.body: Motivated lifters judge themselves healed too early. His arithmetic shows the cost. An injury that needed three weeks costs three if you wait, and about five if you return after two and hurt it again. In the first session back he allows a single set of a single exercise that loads the injured area. If it is fine the next day, one more exercise or set is added, so that any pain can be traced to its cause. Whether an injury has healed is a clinical question. Anything beyond a minor strain, or pain that returns, belongs with a doctor or physiotherapist, and rehabilitation exercises may be needed first.
do: Reintroduce one exercise per session for the injured area and check how it feels the next day.
See a clinician if pain persists, returns or limits daily movement.

entries.title: When time is short, a small dose holds most of your strength
entries.take: A review found younger adults kept strength and size for up to 32 weeks on one session a week and one set per exercise, if loads stayed heavy.
entries.body: A 2021 narrative review of maintenance studies concluded that intensity, meaning relative load, is the variable to keep, while frequency and volume can fall a long way. In younger people strength and muscle size held for up to 32 weeks on as little as one weekly session with one set per exercise. Older adults may need two sessions a week and two to three sets to keep muscle size. The authors found too little data to give figures for athletes. A reduced schedule is therefore a better answer to a busy month than stopping. The conditioning area of this guide gives the matching figures for endurance.
do: In a busy period, keep one or two short sessions with your usual loads and cut the sets.

entries.title: High life stress slowed strength gains and recovery in students
entries.take: In two student studies, people under more life stress gained less strength in 12 weeks and regained force more slowly after a hard leg session.
entries.body: Among 135 undergraduates lifting twice a week for 12 weeks, the low-stress half improved bench press and squat significantly more than the high-stress half. In 31 students given a hard leg press session, higher life-event stress and perceived stress went with slower return of maximal force over the following 96 hours, even after adjusting for fitness, workload and training experience. McDonald's 2010 series gives the coaching version: a plan that suits a calm month can be too much during exams, a breakup or a run of night shifts, with no change to the training itself.
do: In a high-stress stretch, hold or trim training volume and do not add to it.
Leave an extra day between hard sessions for the same muscles when life is rough.

entries.title: Injury restrictions in exam weeks against ordinary weeks
entries.take: Odds of a player having an injury restriction in weeks of high academic stress, in 101 college football players over a season.

entries.title: Allostatic load
entries.take: The cumulative cost to the body of adapting to every stressor it meets. Training, work, short sleep, dieting and emotional strain draw on the same stress response, so they add together.

entries.title: Under-recovery
entries.take: A name some prefer to overtraining. It places the fault in too little sleep, food or rest to absorb the training, and not in the training itself, which may be what the goal requires.

entries.title: When training cannot come down further, raise recovery
entries.take: Every goal needs some minimum amount of training. Once you are near that floor, the lever left is recovery: sleep, food and less outside stress.
entries.body: McDonald's argument is that load can only be cut so far before it stops producing the result you train for, and a competitive goal sets that floor much higher than simply taking part. So when someone is not coping, the question is also what limits recovery. Some limits are fixed, such as age, and call for less training. Others can be changed: sleep, naps, enough food, fewer late nights. A 2021 review adds that preventing under-recovery has many parts but that much of it rests on energy and carbohydrate availability. If recovery improves and the load was already borderline, he keeps the load where it is.
do: Before cutting a programme you need, fix sleep length and daily food intake for two weeks.

entries.title: Cognitive dietary restraint
entries.take: The ongoing, deliberate effort to limit eating in order to control body weight, measured by questionnaire. It describes a mindset and does not always mean eating less.

entries.title: Women who restricted eating most strictly excreted more cortisol
entries.take: In two cross-sectional studies, women with high dietary restraint scores had higher 24-hour urinary cortisol than women with low scores.
entries.body: In 62 young women with normal cycles, the 24-hour urinary cortisol to creatinine ratio was 42.9 with high restraint and 36.3 with low. The high scorers also exercised more and ate less, but cortisol was unrelated to exercise, intake or body size. In 78 postmenopausal women, high scorers excreted 248 nmol a day against 204, with no difference in energy intake, exercise or perceived stress. The authors suggest restraint itself may be a stress. Both studies are snapshots and cannot show cause. McDonald's reading is that strict, anxious dieters start with a higher stress load, and hard dieting and training add to it.
do: If you diet strictly and train hard, count the dieting as part of your stress load.

entries.title: A calorie deficit counts as stress and lowers what you can recover from
entries.take: Calorie restriction raised cortisol in controlled studies, mostly with severe restriction and early on, and deficits blunt what training builds.
entries.body: In 121 women, three weeks at 1,200 kcal a day raised total cortisol output. A meta-analysis of 13 studies with 357 participants found cortisol rose with calorie restriction overall, very strongly with fasting and not significantly with less severe diets, and that it returned to baseline after several weeks. A separate meta-analysis found an energy deficit impaired lean-mass gains from lifting while strength gains held. McDonald treats dieting and training as loads on the same account. His suggestion that cortisol stays high through a long diet is a hypothesis, and the pooled data point to an early, passing rise.
do: Do not raise training volume in the same weeks that you start a diet.
Expect to hold strength on a diet, not to set records.

entries.title: Pairing a steep calorie deficit with large amounts of hard exercise
entries.take: McDonald's rule is to cut calories hard or do a lot of activity, not both. The pairing often stalls and wears people down.
entries.body: He describes very low intakes with hours of often intense cardio, a stalled scale, and a drop in weight once the person eats a little more or trains a little less. One small inpatient study agrees. Twelve overweight women ate about 720 kcal a day for four to five weeks, and six also did 27 hours of moderate cycling over four weeks. Weight loss was the same, 6.9 against 6.5 kg (15.2 and 14.3 lb), and resting oxygen consumption fell a further 17 percent in the exercisers. Physique competitors do pair low calories with much cardio, but get there over months. Other areas of this guide cover low energy availability.
do: With a large deficit, keep lifting and keep cardio modest.
If you want a high training load, use a small deficit.

meeusen-2013.title: Prevention, diagnosis and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: Joint consensus statement of the European College of Sport Science (ECSS) and the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM)
meeusen-2013.support: When athletes do not sufficiently respect the balance between training and recovery, nonfunctional overreaching (NFOR) can occur. The distinction between NFOR and overtraining syndrome (OTS) is very difficult and will depend on the clinical outcome and exclusion diagnosis. Currently, several markers (hormones, performance tests, psychological tests, and biochemical and immune markers) are used, but none of them meet all the criteria to make their use generally accepted.

carrard-2022.title: Diagnosing Overtraining Syndrome: A Scoping Review
carrard-2022.support: Overtraining syndrome (OTS) is a condition characterized by a long-term performance decrement, which occurs after a persisting imbalance between training-related and nontraining-related load and recovery. Because of the lack of a gold standard diagnostic test, OTS remains a diagnosis of exclusion.

kreher-2012.title: Overtraining Syndrome
kreher-2012.support: OTS remains a clinical diagnosis with arbitrary definitions per the European College of Sports Science's position statement. Full text: overreaching requires days to weeks for recovery; nonfunctional overreaching weeks to months; treatment of NFO and OTS is rest.

halson-2004.title: Does Overtraining Exist?
halson-2004.support: Overreaching occurs as a result of intensified training and is often considered a normal outcome for elite athletes due to the relatively short time needed for recovery (approximately 2 weeks). As the time needed to recover from the overtraining syndrome is considered to be much longer (months to years), it may not be appropriate to compare the two states. There is currently no evidence aside from anecdotal information to suggest that overreaching precedes overtraining.

mcdonald-overtraining-1.title: Overtraining, Overreaching and all the Rest Part 1
mcdonald-overtraining-1.support: Backs the points that the overreaching or overtraining label is only known afterwards, that planned hard blocks must be short with recovery after, that elite loads take years to build, and that less is the safer error.

mcdonald-overtraining-3.title: Overtraining, Overreaching and all the Rest Part 3
mcdonald-overtraining-3.support: Backs the stress-against-recovery framing, the minimum training dose argument, the role of job, exam and relationship stress, and his estimate that the syndrome needs months of imbalance.

grandou-2020.title: Overtraining in Resistance Exercise: An Exploratory Systematic Review and Methodological Appraisal of the Literature
grandou-2020.support: A total of 22 studies were selected for review. Among these studies, eight resulted in decrements in performance and measured changes in performance during a follow-up period. A total of 10 studies reported no decline in performance. No marker other than a sustained decrease in performance has been established as a reliable indicator of overtraining in resistance exercise.

bell-2020.title: Overreaching and overtraining in strength sports and resistance training: A scoping review
bell-2020.support: Short-term periods of OR achieved with either high-volume or high-intensity RT can elicit functional OR (FOR) but there is also evidence that chronic high-volume and/or intensity RT can lead to non-functional overreaching (NFOR). There is minimal evidence to suggest that true OTS has occurred in strength sports or RT based on the studies entered during this review.

aubry-2014.title: Functional Overreaching
aubry-2014.support: Eleven of the 23 subjects from the OT group were diagnosed as functionally overreached (F-OR) after the overload period, whereas the 12 other subjects were only acutely fatigued (AF). The AF group demonstrated a small to large greater peak performance supercompensation than the F-OR group (2.6% +/- 1.1%). Ten cases of infection were reported during the study with higher prevalence in F-OR (70%) than that in AF (20%) and CTL (10%).

bellinger-2020.title: Functional Overreaching in Endurance Athletes: A Necessity or Cause for Concern?
bellinger-2020.support: Recent studies have demonstrated dampened training and performance adaptations in FOR athletes compared to non-overreached athletes who completed the same training program or the same relative increase in training load. However, this is not always the case and a number of studies have also demonstrated substantial performance super-compensation in athletes who were classified as being FOR.

mcdonald-overtraining-4.title: Overtraining, Overreaching and all the Rest Part 4
mcdonald-overtraining-4.support: Backs the account of the older sympathetic and parasympathetic typology, the rejection of a clean central and peripheral split, and his reading of the cytokine model of overtraining.

matos-2011.title: Prevalence of Nonfunctional Overreaching/Overtraining in Young English Athletes
matos-2011.support: One hundred ten athletes (29%) reported having been NFOR/OT at least once. Training load was not a significant predictor of NFOR/OT. OT is not solely a training load-related problem with both physical and psychosocial factors identified as important contributors.

smith-2000.title: Cytokine hypothesis of overtraining: a physiological adaptation to excessive stress?
smith-2000.support: It is argued that high volume/intensity training, with insufficient rest, will produce muscle and/or skeletal and/or joint trauma. Elevated circulating cytokines then co-ordinate the whole-body response by communicating with the CNS and inducing a set of behaviors referred to as sickness behavior, which involves mood and behavior changes.

cheng-2020.title: Intramuscular mechanisms of overtraining
cheng-2020.support: Current data implicates reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS) and inflammatory pathways as the most likely mechanisms contributing to OTS in skeletal muscle.

mcdonald-overtraining-6.title: Overtraining, Overeaching and all the Rest Part 6
mcdonald-overtraining-6.support: Backs the morning heart rate method and rule of thumb, his 2010 view of HRV, reaction and jump checks, self-report with a coach's eye, and his plan for resting, eating and rebuilding after a long slump.

stellingwerff-2021.title: Overtraining Syndrome (OTS) and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S): Shared Pathways, Symptoms and Complexities
stellingwerff-2021.support: Eighteen of the 21 studies (86%) that met our criteria showed indications of an EA decrease or difference between two cohorts within a given study (n = 14 studies) or CHO availability decrease (n = 4 studies) during the training-overload/OTS period, resulting in both training-overload/OTS and RED-S symptom outcomes compared to control conditions.

mcdonald-overtraining-2.title: Overtraining, Overreaching and all the Rest Part 2
mcdonald-overtraining-2.support: Backs judging by a trend in performance and effort and not by one session, the point that lab markers are impractical, and the view that submaximal work can be ground through while maximal work fails outright.

saw-2016.title: Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review
saw-2016.support: Fifty-six original studies reported concurrent subjective and objective measures of athlete well-being. Subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training loads with superior sensitivity and consistency than objective measures.

hausswirth-2014.title: Evidence of Disturbed Sleep and Increased Illness in Overreached Endurance Athletes
hausswirth-2014.support: Only the F-OR group demonstrated a decrease in these three parameters (-7.9% +/- 6.7%, -1.6% +/- 0.7%, and -7.6% +/- 6.6% for SD, SE, and IT, respectively), which was reversed during the subsequent taper phase. Higher prevalence of upper respiratory tract infections were also reported in F-OR (67%, 22%, and 11% incidence rate for F-OR, AF, and CTL, respectively).

bellenger-2016.title: Monitoring Athletic Training Status Through Autonomic Heart Rate Regulation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
bellenger-2016.support: Increases in post-exercise HRV and HRR also occur in response to overreaching, demonstrating that additional measures of training tolerance may be required to determine whether training-induced changes in these parameters are related to positive or negative adaptations. Resting HRV is largely unaffected by overreaching, although this may be the result of methodological issues that warrant further investigation.

manresa-rocamora-2021.title: Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training for Enhancing Cardiac-Vagal Modulation, Aerobic Fitness, and Endurance Performance: A Methodological Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
manresa-rocamora-2021.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
manresa-rocamora-2021.support: If HRV-guided training is superior to predefined training for producing group-level improvements in fitness and performance, current data suggest it is only by a small margin.

duking-2021.title: Monitoring and adapting endurance training on the basis of heart rate variability monitored by wearable technologies: A systematic review with meta-analysis
duking-2021.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
duking-2021.support: A total of 8 studies (198 participants) were identified. In comparison to predefined training, HRV-guided endurance training had a medium-sized effect on submaximal physiological parameters, but only a small and non-significant influence on performance and VO2peak. There were fewer non-responders regarding performance with HRV-based training.

de-oliveira-2019.title: Effect of individualized resistance training prescription with heart rate variability on individual muscle hypertrophy and strength responses
de-oliveira-2019.support: Twenty young men were randomized in the RT-IND and RT-FIX groups. 1-RM values increased significantly from pre to post-training for both groups (RT-IND: 30% and RT-FIX: 42%), with no significant difference between groups. Muscle CSA increased significantly (RT-IND: 15.7% and RT-FIX: 15.8%), with no significant difference between groups.

duignan-2020.title: Single-Item Self-Report Measures of Team-Sport Athlete Wellbeing and Their Relationship With Training Load: A Systematic Review
duignan-2020.support: A total of 21 studies were included in the analysis. The measures used most frequently were muscle soreness, fatigue, sleep quality, stress, and mood. All measures presented various relationships with metrics of training load from no association to a very large association.

mcdonald-overtraining-5.title: Overtraining, Overeaching and all the Rest Part 5
mcdonald-overtraining-5.support: Backs the weekly day off, the cap on truly hard days, the planned five-day and yearly breaks, and the rule of using the warm-up to decide a doubtful session.

claudino-2017.title: The countermovement jump to monitor neuromuscular status: A meta-analysis
claudino-2017.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
claudino-2017.support: 151 articles were included providing a total of 531 ESs for the meta-analyses. Based on the meta-analysis, average CMJ height was more sensitive than highest CMJ height in detecting CMJ fatigue and supercompensation.

nederhof-2006.title: Psychomotor Speed
nederhof-2006.support: NFO and OTS could be prevented using early markers, which should be objective, not manipulable, applicable in training practice, not too demanding, affordable and should be based on a sound theoretical framework. No such markers exist up to today. It is proposed that psychomotor speed might be such a marker.

mcdonald-supercompensation.title: The Facts About Supercompensation of Training
mcdonald-supercompensation.support: Backs the argument that deplete-and-overshoot fits glycogen only, that fitness and fatigue is the better description, and that sessions overlap without full recovery; also his criticism of the general adaptation syndrome.

hellard-2006.title: Assessing the limitations of the Banister model in monitoring training
hellard-2006.support: The training loads of nine elite swimmers, measured over one season, were related to performances with the Banister model. Performances were related to training loads for all participants (R2 = 0.79 +/- 0.13). Nevertheless, the range of 95% CI values of the most useful parameters for monitoring training was wide.

buckner-2020.title: The Basics of Training for Muscle Size and Strength: A Brief Review on the Theory
buckner-2020.support: Hans Selye conducted a series of rodent studies which used toxic stressors to facilitate the development of the general adaptation syndrome. To our knowledge, normal exercise in humans has never been shown to produce a general adaptation syndrome.

cunanan-2018.title: The General Adaptation Syndrome: A Foundation for the Concept of Periodization
cunanan-2018.support: Disturbance to the state of an organism is the driving force for biological adaptation, which is the central thesis of the GAS model and the primary basis for its application to the athlete's training process. Despite its imprecisions, the GAS has proven to be an instructive framework.

kataoka-2022.title: Is there Evidence for the Suggestion that Fatigue Accumulates Following Resistance Exercise?
kataoka-2022.support: Overall, evidence for the presence of fatigue accumulation with resistance training is equivocal, making it difficult to draw the conclusion that fatigue accumulates.

damas-2016-synthesis.title: Resistance training-induced changes in integrated myofibrillar protein synthesis are related to hypertrophy only after attenuation of muscle damage
damas-2016-synthesis.support: Muscle damage (Z-band streaming) was the highest during post-RE recovery at T1, lower at T2 and minimal at T3. When muscle damage was the highest, so was the integrated MyoPS (at T1), but neither were related to hypertrophy; however, integrated MyoPS at T2 and T3 were correlated with hypertrophy.

kiely-2018.title: Periodization Theory: Confronting an Inconvenient Truth
kiely-2018.support: If the original scientific platform upon which periodization theory was founded has disintegrated, should we critically re-evaluate conventional perspectives through an updated conceptual lens?

mcdonald-importance-of-rest.title: The Importance of Rest
mcdonald-importance-of-rest.support: Backs one full rest day a week for everyone, three to four training days for most recreational lifters, and breaks of five days or more after long training blocks.

mcdonald-active-passive-recovery.title: Active Versus Passive Recovery
mcdonald-active-passive-recovery.support: Backs the definitions of active and passive rest, his volume and intensity guide for an easy session, its use for technique, and the warning that easy days drift into workouts.

dupuy-2018.title: An Evidence-Based Approach for Choosing Post-exercise Recovery Techniques to Reduce Markers of Muscle Damage, Soreness, Fatigue, and Inflammation: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
dupuy-2018.support: Overall, 99 studies were included. Active recovery, massage, compression garments, immersion, contrast water therapy, and cryotherapy induced a small to large decrease (-2.26 < g < -0.40) in the magnitude of DOMS, while there was no change for the other methods. Massage was found to be the most powerful technique for recovering from DOMS and fatigue.

ortiz-2019.title: A Systematic Review on the Effectiveness of Active Recovery Interventions on Athletic Performance of Professional-, Collegiate-, and Competitive-Level Adult Athletes
ortiz-2019.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
ortiz-2019.support: Twenty-six articles involving 471 subjects remained after full analysis. The review suggests that there are positive psychological outcomes from AR sessions, a need to determine if AR should be individualized in its application, and weak evidence regarding the efficacy of postexercise AR, particularly relating to performance.

rogerson-2024.title: Deloading Practices in Strength and Physique Sports: A Cross-sectional Survey
rogerson-2024.support: The typical duration of a deload was 6.4 ± 1.7 days, integrated into the training programme every 5.6 ± 2.3 weeks.

mcdonald-hard-easy.title: Keep the Hard Days Hard and the Easy Days Easy: Part 1
mcdonald-hard-easy.support: Backs the argument that easy days done too hard pull the whole week toward medium effort, and that hard and easy periods alternate over days, weeks and blocks.

foster-1998.title: Monitoring training in athletes with reference to overtraining syndrome
foster-1998.support: Studies in animal models have suggested that unremittingly heavy training (monotonous training) may increase the likelihood of developing overtraining syndrome. It was observed that a high percentage of illnesses could be accounted for when individual athletes exceeded individually identifiable training thresholds, mostly related to the strain of training.

mcdonald-hlm.title: Heavy Light Medium Training
mcdonald-hlm.support: Backs the description of heavy, light and medium days, the load ranges for the lighter days, the ways to lighten a day, and the options for ordering and staggering the heavy work.

moran-navarro-2017.title: Time course of recovery following resistance training leading or not to failure
moran-navarro-2017.support: Ten resistance-trained men undertook three RT protocols. Recovery from the 3 x 5(10) and 6 x 5(10) protocols was significantly faster between 24 and 48 h post-exercise compared to 3 x 10(10). Training to failure slows down recovery up to 24-48 h post-exercise.

mcdonald-two-a-day-1.title: Two a Day Training in the Weight Room Part 1
mcdonald-two-a-day-1.support: Backs his reasons for training the same muscles twice in a day, the four to six hour gap, the short starting sessions and the rule that one session is heavy and the other light.

hartman-2007-twice.title: Comparisons Between Twice-Daily and Once-Daily Training Sessions in Male Weight Lifters
hartman-2007-twice.journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
hartman-2007-twice.support: Ten nationally competitive male weightlifters were randomly assigned to train either once or twice daily for 3 wk. There were no additional benefits from increased daily training frequency in national-level male weightlifters, but the increase in ISO and EMG activity for the twice-daily group might provide some rationale for dividing training load.

correa-2022.title: Twice-daily sessions result in a greater muscle strength and a similar muscle hypertrophy compared to once-daily session in resistance-trained men
correa-2022.journal: The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness
correa-2022.support: The increase in 1RM back squat was significantly greater in 2S (16.1%) compared to 1S (7.8%). Both groups significantly increased bench press 1RM, back squat 60% 1RM, bench press 60% 1RM and all MT outcomes, with no differences between experimental groups.

hansen-2005.title: Skeletal muscle adaptation: training twice every second day vs. training once daily
hansen-2005.support: Seven healthy untrained men performed knee extensor exercise with one leg trained in a low-glycogen (Low) protocol and the other leg trained at a high-glycogen (High) protocol. Time until exhaustion at 90% was markedly more increased in the Low leg compared with the High leg. The present study suggests that training twice every second day may be superior to daily training.

mcdonald-two-a-day-2.title: Two a Day Training in the Weight Room Part 2
mcdonald-two-a-day-2.support: Backs the points that the gap between sessions is flexible and that which session is heavy depends on the lifter and the time of day.

mcdonald-six-days.title: Lifting 6 Days Per Week for Mass Gains
mcdonald-six-days.support: Backs the six-day layout: an upper and lower rotation, a few work sets per session, reps kept in reserve early in the week, and a periodic unloading.

colquhoun-2018.title: Training Volume, Not Frequency, Indicative of Maximal Strength Adaptations to Resistance Training
colquhoun-2018.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
colquhoun-2018.support: Twenty-eight young, healthy resistance-trained men were randomly assigned to either 3x per week or 6x per week. It seems that increased training frequency does not lead to additional strength improvements when volume and intensity are equated.

cheung-2003.title: Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness
cheung-2003.support: DOMS is most prevalent at the beginning of the sporting season when athletes are returning to training following a period of reduced activity. DOMS can affect athletic performance by causing a reduction in joint range of motion, shock attenuation and peak torque.

mcdonald-doms.title: DOMS and Muscle Growth
mcdonald-doms.support: Backs his observations that soreness is worst when growth is least, that muscles trained more often get less sore yet grow, and that damage beyond a moderate amount works against progress.

mchugh-2003.title: Recent advances in the understanding of the repeated bout effect: the protective effect against muscle damage from a single bout of eccentric exercise
mchugh-2003.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
mchugh-2003.support: The repeated bout effect refers to the adaptation whereby a single bout of eccentric exercise protects against muscle damage from subsequent eccentric bouts.

chen-2006.title: Responses of Elbow Flexors to Two Strenuous Eccentric Exercise Bouts Separated by Three Days
chen-2006.journal: The Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
chen-2006.support: Fifty-one athletes performed 30 eccentric actions of the elbow flexors. No significant differences between the control group and other groups indicate that the second eccentric exercise performed 3 days after the initial bout does not exacerbate muscle damage and retard the recovery regardless of the intensity of the second bout.

nosaka-2002.title: Delayed‐onset muscle soreness does not reflect the magnitude of eccentric exercise‐induced muscle damage
nosaka-2002.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
nosaka-2002.support: Male students (n = 110) performed 12 (12ECC), 24 (24ECC), or 60 maximal eccentric actions of the elbow flexors (60ECC). Because of generally poor correlations between DOMS and other indicators, we conclude that use of DOMS is a poor reflector of eccentric exercise-induced muscle damage and inflammation, and changes in indirect markers of muscle damage and inflammation are not necessarily accompanied with DOMS.

rawson-2017.title: Perspectives on Exertional Rhabdomyolysis
rawson-2017.support: Exertional (exercise-induced) rhabdomyolysis is a potentially life threatening condition. Although the prevalence of rhabdomyolysis is low, instances still occur where exercise is improperly prescribed or used as punishment. Full text: a cardinal sign that an individual should seek immediate treatment is dark-colored urine.

bosquet-2013.title: Effect of training cessation on muscular performance: A meta-analysis
bosquet-2013.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
bosquet-2013.support: Seven databases were searched from which 103 of 284 potential studies met inclusion criteria. A dose-response relationship between the amplitude of SMD and the duration of training cessation was identified. The effect of resistance training cessation was found to be larger in older people (> 65 years old). The effect was also larger in inactive people for maximal force and maximal power when compared with recreational athletes.

cumming-2024.title: Muscle memory in humans: evidence for myonuclear permanence and long-term transcriptional regulation after strength training
cumming-2024.support: Twelve untrained men and women performed 10 weeks of unilateral elbow-flexor strength training followed by 16 weeks of de-training. The sustained higher number of myonuclei in the previously trained muscle confirms myonuclear accretion and permanence in humans. Nevertheless, because of the unclear effect on the subsequent hypertrophy with re-training, the physiological benefit remains to be determined.

rahmati-2022.title: Myonuclear permanence in skeletal muscle memory: a systematic review and meta-analysis of human and animal studies
rahmati-2022.journal: Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle
rahmati-2022.support: The major finding from the present meta-analysis is that myonuclei are not permanent but are lost during periods of atrophy and with ageing. These findings do not support the concept of skeletal muscle memory based on the permanence of myonuclei.

mcdonald-training-after-layoff.title: Returning to Training After a Layoff
mcdonald-training-after-layoff.support: Backs his rules by length of break: nothing lost in a few days, roughly twice the break length to regain form after one to two weeks, restart as a beginner after months, and the injury rules of an extra week and one exercise at a time.

travis-2022.title: The Effects of 3 vs. 5 Days of Training Cessation on Maximal Strength
travis-2022.support: Nineteen strength-trained athletes ... maximal lower-body strength can be preserved during 3 and 5 days of training cessation, but maximal upper-body strength is only preserved for 3 days after 4 weeks of strength training in athletes.

hwang-2017.title: Resistance Training-Induced Elevations in Muscular Strength in Trained Men Are Maintained After 2 Weeks of Detraining and Not Differentially Affected by Whey Protein Supplementation
hwang-2017.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
hwang-2017.support: Twenty resistance-trained men were randomized. LPS was elevated throughout the 10-week training study with no decrease in LPS after DT in both groups. A 2-week period of DT appeared to retain muscular strength in resistance-trained men.

psilander-2019.title: Effects of training, detraining, and retraining on strength, hypertrophy, and myonuclear number in human skeletal muscle
psilander-2019.support: Nine men and 10 women performed unilateral strength training (T1) for 10 wk, followed by 20 wk of detraining (DT) and a 5-wk bilateral retraining period (T2). MT and CSA returned to baseline values during DT, but strength remained elevated. In conclusion, training response during T2 did not differ between the mem-leg and con-leg.

ogasawara-2013.title: Comparison of muscle hypertrophy following 6-month of continuous and periodic strength training
ogasawara-2013.support: 14 young men were randomly divided into a CTR group and a PTR group. The results indicate that 3-week detraining/6-week retraining cycles result in muscle hypertrophy similar to that occurring with continuous resistance training after 24 weeks.

halonen-2024.title: Does Taking a Break Matter: Adaptations in Muscle Strength and Size Between Continuous and Periodic Resistance Training
halonen-2024.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
halonen-2024.support: PRT completed a 10-week RT, a 10-week detraining, and a second identical 10-week RT. PRT and CTR ended up in similar postintervention adaptations, as decreased muscle strength and size during detraining in PRT regained rapidly during retraining.

staron-1991.title: Strength and skeletal muscle adaptations in heavy-resistance-trained women after detraining and retraining
staron-1991.support: Six women who had participated in a previous 20-wk strength training study for the lower limb detrained for 30-32 wk and subsequently retrained for 6 wk. Detraining had relatively little effect on fiber cross-sectional area. Maximal dynamic strength decreased but not to pretraining levels.

mcdonald-returning-from-my-layoff.title: Returning From My Layoff
mcdonald-returning-from-my-layoff.support: Backs the worked example of restarting after about five months off: very short sessions of one light high-rep set, with sets, load and then lower reps added over several weeks.

spiering-2021.title: Maintaining Physical Performance: The Minimal Dose of Exercise Needed to Preserve Endurance and Strength Over Time
spiering-2021.support: Endurance performance can be maintained for up to 15 weeks when training frequency is reduced to as little as 2 sessions per week or when exercise volume is reduced by 33-66%, as long as exercise intensity is maintained. Strength and muscle size (at least in younger populations) can be maintained for up to 32 weeks with as little as 1 session of strength training per week and 1 set per exercise, as long as exercise intensity (relative load) is maintained.

bartholomew-2008.title: Strength Gains after Resistance Training: The Effect of Stressful, Negative Life Events
bartholomew-2008.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
bartholomew-2008.support: Participants were 135 undergraduates enrolled in weight training classes that met for 1.5 hours, two times per week. Results indicated that the low stress participants experienced a significantly greater increase in bench press and squat than their high stress counterparts.

stults-kolehmainen-2014.title: Chronic Psychological Stress Impairs Recovery of Muscular Function and Somatic Sensations Over a 96-Hour Period
stults-kolehmainen-2014.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
stults-kolehmainen-2014.support: Stress, whether assessed as life event stress or perceived stress, moderated the recovery trajectories of muscular function and somatic sensations in a 96-hour period after strenuous resistance exercise. In all analyses, higher stress was associated with worse recovery.

mann-2016.title: Effect of Physical and Academic Stress on Illness and Injury in Division 1 College Football Players
mann-2016.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
mann-2016.support: The odds of an injury restriction during weeks of HAS were nearly twice as high as during weeks of LAS (OR = 1.78, p = 0.0088).

mcewen-2000.title: Allostasis and Allostatic Load Implications for Neuropsychopharmacology
mcewen-2000.support: The primary hormonal mediators of the stress response, glucocorticoids and catecholamines, have both protective and damaging effects on the body. In the short run, they are essential for adaptation, maintenance of homeostasis, and survival (allostasis). Yet, over longer time intervals, they exact a cost (allostatic load) that can accelerate disease processes.

mclean-2001.title: Cognitive dietary restraint is associated with higher urinary cortisol excretion in healthy premenopausal women
mclean-2001.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
mclean-2001.support: Ratios of urinary cortisol (nmol) to creatinine (mmol) were higher in the high-restraint than in the low-restraint group (42.9+/-12.9 compared with 36.3+/-8.9; P<0.05). Urinary cortisol was not associated with exercise, nutrient intakes, or anthropometric measurements.

rideout-2006.title: High Cognitive Dietary Restraint Is Associated With Increased Cortisol Excretion in Postmenopausal Women
rideout-2006.journal: The Journals of Gerontology Series A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
rideout-2006.support: Urinary cortisol excretion was higher in the high restraint group (248.2 +/- 61.7 nmol/d vs 204.3 +/- 66.1 nmol/d; p =.01). Women with high or low dietary restraint did not differ in age, body mass index, waist-to-hip ratio, energy intake, perceived stress, current exercise, or measures of body composition.

mcdonald-restraint-cortisol.title: Dietary Restraint and Cortisol Levels - Research Review
mcdonald-restraint-cortisol.support: Backs his reading of the restraint and cortisol study and his advice that strict dieters who stall should ease off instead of dieting harder.

tomiyama-2010.title: Low Calorie Dieting Increases Cortisol
tomiyama-2010.support: 121 female participants were assigned randomly to one of four dietary interventions for 3 weeks. Restricting calories (1200 kcal/day) increased the total output of cortisol.

nakamura-2016.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis reveals acutely elevated plasma cortisol following fasting but not less severe calorie restriction
nakamura-2016.support: Overall, caloric restriction significantly increased serum cortisol level in 13 studies (357 total participants). Fasting showed a very strong effect in increasing serum cortisol, while VLCD and LCD did not show significant increases. Serum cortisol is increased in the initial period of caloric restriction but decreased to the baseline level after several weeks.

murphy-2021.title: Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: A meta‐analysis and meta‐regression
murphy-2021.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
murphy-2021.support: Meta-regression: an energy deficit of ~500 kcal/day prevented gains in lean mass; strength gains were comparable between conditions.

mcdonald-low-calories-exercise.title: Big Caloric Deficits, Lots of Activity and Fat Loss
mcdonald-low-calories-exercise.support: Backs his rule that a steep deficit and a large exercise load should not be combined, and his hypothesis that the combined stress is the reason.

phinney-1988.title: Effects of aerobic exercise on energy expenditure and nitrogen balance during very low calorie dieting
phinney-1988.support: The resting oxygen consumption (rVO2) of both groups declined 10% in the first seven days of dieting. Thereafter the rVO2 in group 1 remained stable, but a further 17% reduction occurred in group 2 by the third week of exercise. Weight loss over 4 weeks in the two groups did not differ.
